title: About 8 in 10 Americans take supplements, and many see them as important to their health
summary: About eight-in-ten U.S. adults say they are currently taking at least one supplement for their health, according to a new Pew Research Center survey.

title: The U.S. Electorate’s Changing Racial and Ethnic Makeup
summary: The share of eligible voters who are White has declined since 2006, while the Hispanic and Asian shares have nearly doubled. The share of Black eligible voters has changed little over the same period.

title: 25 Years After 9/11, a Portrait of Muslim Americans
summary: Some Americans still see Muslims through the lens of the terrorist attacks. Yet Muslims are a growing, vibrant part of the country’s political and religious landscape.

title: 9/11 memories remain vivid in the U.S. 25 years later
summary: While 9/11 remains vivid in most Americans’ memories, 10% of adults today were born after the attacks and learned about the day’s events from others.

title: Americans have grown more skeptical that a woman will be president in their lifetime
summary: Some 37% of Americans now say it’s not too or not at all likely that the United States will elect a woman as president, up from 26% in 2023.

title: About half of Americans say they spend too much time on their smartphone
summary: Seven-in-ten adults under 30 say they spend too much time on their smartphone, as do about two-thirds of those ages 30 to 49.

title: What the ‘American dream’ means to U.S. Latinos, in their own words
summary: The phrase “the American dream” has long been used to describe hopes associated with life in the United States. Over time, it has come to encompass many ideals, including economic mobility, homeownership, political freedoms and equality. A Pew Research Center survey finds that U.S. Latinos are divided on whether they can achieve the American dream. […]

title: How immigrant and U.S.-born Latinos see economic mobility and the American dream
summary: Latinos in the United States broadly view living standards as improving across generations – both when looking back at their parents and looking ahead for their children. Overall, immigrant Latinos hold more positive views about intergenerational economic progress than those born in the U.S. At the same time, immigrants are less likely than the U.S. […]

title: Latinos Are Split on Whether the American Dream Is Achievable
summary: Far more Latinos say their standard of living is better than their parents’ (57%), rather than worse (23%). More also say their children’s standard of living will be better than their own (53%) as opposed to worse (14%).

title: Who Sees Themselves as Working Class?
